text: Here's a quirk that surprises developers moving onto Oracle for the first time: you can't just select an expression on its own. Oracle wants a FROM clause, every time, even when there's no real table involved. This lesson is about why, and what DUAL actually is.

Select one plus one, with nothing else, is a syntax error on Oracle. Oracle's grammar requires a FROM clause on every SELECT statement, full stop. The fix is select one plus one FROM DUAL — and DUAL is not a trick or a keyword, it's a genuine built-in system table with exactly one row and one column, shipped specifically to satisfy this rule.

And DUAL is actually useful day to day — select SYSDATE from DUAL gets you the current date, select UPPER of hello from DUAL evaluates a string function, select two times three from DUAL does simple math. Any time you want to evaluate an expression with no real table behind it, DUAL from Oracle is how you do it.

SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all skip this requirement entirely. Select one plus one, select GETDATE, select NOW — none of them need a FROM clause at all. There's no DUAL-style workaround needed because the grammar never demanded one in the first place.

Interestingly, MySQL goes out of its way to accept FROM DUAL anyway, purely as a courtesy for people and scripts coming over from Oracle — even though MySQL's own syntax never required it. Next lesson: comments and statement terminators, including what GO actually is and isn't.
